cards.front: In a colon-style switch, is int temp = 10; inside case 1 legal?
cards.back: Yes — it is the first declaration of temp in the switch block's single scope.
cards.extra: A colon-style switch has one shared scope for the whole block. Declaring temp in case 1 is fine because the name is not taken yet; trouble starts only if another case declares it again.
cards.example:
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        int temp = 10;   // legal: first temp in the switch scope
        System.out.println(temp);
        break;
}

cards.front: In that same colon-style switch, is int temp = 20; inside case 2 legal?
cards.back: No — temp is already in the shared switch scope, so this is a duplicate local variable compile-time error.
cards.extra: Case labels do not create scopes. Both declarations belong to the one switch block, so the second int temp collides with the first even though you read the cases as separate branches.
cards.example:
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        int temp = 10;
        break;
    case 2:
        int temp = 20;   // compile error: temp is already defined in the switch block
        break;
}

cards.front: Why can't a colon-style switch case safely reuse a variable declared in an earlier case?
cards.back: Control may jump straight to that case, so the earlier declaration never ran and the variable is uninitialised.
cards.extra: Case labels are jump targets, not sequential steps. Entering at case 2 skips int temp = 10; in case 1, so reading temp there fails with 'variable might not have been initialized'.
cards.example:
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        int temp = 10;
        break;
    case 2:
        // System.out.println(temp);  // compile error: temp may not have been initialized
        break;
}

cards.front: What scope does an arrow case body case L -> { ... } get in a switch expression?
cards.back: Its own block scope — the same local name may be redeclared in another case.
cards.extra: Each arrow body is a separate block, so variables declared inside it live only until its closing brace. That is what removes the name-collision problem of the colon form.
cards.example:
int result = switch (day) {
    case 1 -> {
        int temp = 10;   // local to case 1
        yield temp * 2;
    }
    case 2 -> {
        int temp = 20;   // valid: a different local variable
        yield temp * 3;
    }
    default -> 0;
};
